canonical_topic: Earnings manipulation risk via MTM on illiquid assets
definition: Because MTM relies on trading market prices, it is only safe for liquid markets with enough trading activity to keep prices rational; for illiquid assets, traders can potentially manipulate reported P&L by transacting at artificial prices.
core_idea: The author illustrates this with two traders at rival firms who, to avoid reporting losses to their risk committee, each buy a small amount of an illiquid asset the other holds at an inflated price — letting the counterparty mark a profit — without ever having to trade with each other directly; doing this across many small, illiquid positions can be hard to detect.
key_points: MTM is only reliable in liquid markets with enough trading volume to produce rational prices.
For illiquid assets, it can be necessary to supplement market prices with pricing models as a second check.
That second check both limits the risk of transacting at illogical prices and limits traders' ability to manipulate MTM to smooth earnings.

Example scheme: two traders each buy a small amount of an illiquid asset the OTHER holds, at a high price, letting each mark a profit on their own illiquid holding without directly trading with each other.
The trade size needed to set the price can be very small, and spreading this across many illiquid, unowned assets can make the manipulation hard to catch.
This type of abuse is mitigated by comparing trades/marks against a modeled price rather than relying on market price alone.
relationships: Ties back to Mark-to-Market Accounting's dependence on real trading markets, and to the fair value hierarchy accounting has developed for illiquid/heavily modeled prices.
trading_implications: Risk committees and firms should require a modeled-price cross-check for illiquid marks, not just the latest trade, to prevent traders from using small collusive trades to manage reported earnings and avoid loss-driven trading curtailment or bonus impacts.
caveats: A reported MTM profit isn't proof of real economic value if the market behind it is illiquid and the price was set by a small, possibly collusive trade.
